subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The Hubble Sequence
description: A 60-second lesson on The Hubble Sequence.

hook.text: Edwin Hubble classified galaxies by shape in the 1920s. His tuning-fork diagram is still used today.

buildup.text: Ellipticals sit at one end, spirals branch into barred and unbarred types, and irregulars fall off the chart.

discovery.text: Hubble thought galaxies evolved along the sequence—ellipticals turning into spirals. He was wrong, but the classification stuck.

twist.text: We now know spirals can merge into ellipticals, not the other way around. Evolution runs opposite to Hubble's guess.

climax.text: Modern surveys classify millions of galaxies. Citizen scientists helped through the Galaxy Zoo project.

punchline.text: A wrong guess, but a lasting framework. Hubble's fork still organizes the cosmos.

quiz.question: What did Hubble get wrong about his galaxy classification?
options: He thought galaxies evolved from elliptical to spiral, but the reverse is true
He believed all galaxies were the same size
He classified spiral galaxies as irregular

details.summary: The Hubble sequence (or tuning fork diagram) is Edwin Hubble's classification scheme for galaxies based on shape: ellipticals (E0-E7), lenticulars (S0), and spirals (Sa-Sc, with barred variants SBa-SBc).
details.whyItMatters: The Hubble sequence provides the vocabulary for discussing galaxy types. Understanding why galaxies have different shapes reveals their formation histories, merger records, and star formation patterns.
takeaways: Classifies galaxies by shape: elliptical, lenticular, spiral
Known as the tuning fork diagram from its visual layout
Still the standard framework for galaxy morphology

faq.question: Do galaxies evolve along the Hubble sequence?
faq.answer: Not in the way Hubble initially speculated. Galaxies don't smoothly evolve from elliptical to spiral. Instead, galaxy mergers can transform spirals into ellipticals through violent gravitational interactions.

faq.question: Where do irregular galaxies fit in the Hubble sequence?
faq.answer: Irregulars don't fit the main sequence — they're classified separately. They lack the symmetry of ellipticals or spirals, often due to gravitational interactions with neighboring galaxies. The Magellanic Clouds are irregular galaxies. About 20% of known galaxies are classified as irregular.
